questions.stem: Organisational psychology is best defined as:
options: the treatment of mental illness in people who are unable to work because of their symptoms
the study of the legal rights of employees and the laws governing workplace contracts
the evidence-based study of organisations and the performance and satisfaction of their members
the study of how to increase an organisation's profits through advertising and marketing campaigns
questions.explanation: Organisational psychology uses research evidence to understand and improve work performance and job satisfaction at the individual, group and organisational levels.

questions.stem: At which three levels does organisational psychology consider the factors affecting work?
options: the brain, the body and the nervous system
the manager, the customer and the shareholder
the individual, the team and the organisation
the family, the school and the wider community
questions.explanation: Organisational psychologists look at individuals, teams and whole organisations, since factors at each level affect performance and job satisfaction.

questions.stem: A local council, a supermarket chain and a charity that runs food banks are examples of which three types of organisation, in order?
options: commercial, government and not-for-profit
not-for-profit, commercial and government
government, not-for-profit and commercial
government, commercial and not-for-profit
questions.explanation: Councils are government organisations, supermarket chains are commercial businesses run for profit, and charities are not-for-profit organisations.

questions.stem: A hospital, a school and a bank are all classified as which kind of organisation, based on the work they do?
options: mining industries
farming industries
service industries
manufacturing industries
questions.explanation: Organisations can be classified by type of work. Health care, education and banking provide services rather than extracting resources or making goods.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a measure of individual performance?
options: the total sales made by a regional team
a supervisor's rating of an employee's work
the annual profit made by the whole company
the staff turnover rate across the organisation
questions.explanation: Supervisor ratings and the quantity and quality of a person's work measure individual performance. Profit and turnover are organisational measures, and team sales are a group measure.

questions.stem: What is a main disadvantage of supervisor ratings as a measure of individual performance?
options: They cannot be used for any jobs in service industries
They measure only the profit of the whole organisation
They are always identical for every employee in a team
They can be biased by a supervisor's impressions
questions.explanation: Supervisor ratings can capture aspects of work that are hard to count, but they are subjective and open to biases such as the halo effect or favouritism.

questions.stem: An organisation has high profits but very high staff turnover. Why might an organisational psychologist be concerned?
options: Staff turnover only matters in not-for-profit and government organisations
Turnover is a measure of individual performance, not of the organisation
Turnover suggests low satisfaction and adds hiring and training costs
High profits always mean that employees are satisfied with their jobs
questions.explanation: No single measure gives the full picture. High turnover can signal problems such as poor conditions or low satisfaction, and replacing staff is costly, which may threaten future performance.

questions.stem: What is a disadvantage of using quantity of work, such as the number of calls handled, as a performance measure?
options: It may ignore the quality of the work done
It cannot be counted or recorded objectively
It is a measure of group rather than individual work
It is always biased by a supervisor's opinions
questions.explanation: Counting output is objective, but it can encourage speed at the expense of quality, such as rushing calls without solving customers' problems.

questions.stem: Vocational guidance refers to:
options: training managers to lead teams better
helping a person find a suitable job
selecting the best applicant for a vacancy
measuring the profit of an organisation
questions.explanation: Vocational guidance helps individuals identify suitable careers, often by assessing their interests. Choosing among applicants is personnel selection.

questions.stem: Holland's theory of vocational interests describes six types. Which list is correct?
options: realistic, intellectual, artistic, sociable, energetic, careful
rational, investigative, active, social, enterprising, creative
realistic, investigative, assertive, social, extraverted, conventional
realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising, conventional
questions.explanation: Holland's six types are realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising and conventional, often shortened to RIASEC.

questions.stem: A student who enjoys working with tools, machines and outdoor tasks would most likely score highest on which Holland type?
options: social
conventional
realistic
artistic
questions.explanation: The realistic type prefers practical, hands-on work with tools, machines or animals. Social types prefer helping people, and conventional types prefer organised, data-based tasks.

questions.stem: A person whose Self-Directed Search code is SAE is most likely to be suited to which job?
options: a counsellor or teacher
a mechanic or electrician
an accountant or auditor
a laboratory scientist
questions.explanation: Social is the highest type, followed by artistic and enterprising, which suits work helping and teaching people. A mechanic fits realistic, an accountant fits conventional, and a laboratory scientist fits investigative.

questions.stem: How is Holland's Self-Directed Search used to provide vocational guidance?
options: It assesses mental health so the person can be referred for treatment
It ranks job applicants so an employer can select the best one
It scores interests to give a three-letter code matched to occupations
It measures intelligence so the person can be matched to a salary
questions.explanation: The person completes the inventory, which produces a code of their three strongest interest types. Occupations with similar codes are suggested, on the idea that people are more satisfied in jobs matching their interests.

questions.stem: Personnel selection is the process of:
options: measuring whether a team is meeting its targets
creating a culture that employees will enjoy
finding the right person for a particular job
helping a person find a career that suits them
questions.explanation: Personnel selection is the organisation's side of matching people and jobs: choosing the applicant most likely to perform well.

questions.stem: A job advertisement asks for a 'young, energetic salesman'. Why might this language preclude finding the right person for the job?
options: It makes the job sound too attractive, so too many people apply
It attracts only applicants with university qualifications
It may discourage capable older and female applicants from applying
It describes the skills needed for the job in far too much detail
questions.explanation: Words that imply age or gender can put off suitable applicants and may be discriminatory. Neutral, skills-based language widens the pool of qualified candidates.

questions.stem: Which characteristic is most relevant to consider when selecting the right person for a job?
options: the person's qualifications and experience for the role
the person's ethnicity, as it predicts work performance
the person's age, as older people are always less productive
the person's gender, as some jobs suit only one gender
questions.explanation: Qualifications, experience, abilities, personality and interests relevant to the job help predict performance. Using ethnicity, age or gender as a basis for decisions is biased and generally unlawful.

questions.stem: Which statement about interviews in personnel selection is best supported by research?
options: Structured interviews are usually more reliable and valid than unstructured ones
Unstructured interviews are more valid because the interviewer can follow hunches
All interviews have perfect validity because applicants answer face to face
Interviews cannot be used together with any other selection assessment
questions.explanation: Structured interviews ask every applicant the same job-related questions and score answers against set criteria, which reduces bias and improves reliability and validity. Unstructured interviews are more open to first impressions and the halo effect.

questions.stem: An interviewer rates an applicant highly on every quality because the applicant is well dressed and confident. This is an example of:
options: the norm of reciprocity
the halo effect
the recency effect
stereotype threat
questions.explanation: The halo effect occurs when one positive characteristic influences judgements of unrelated qualities. It can reduce the validity of interviews.

questions.stem: A psychological test used in selection gives similar scores when applicants retake it, but scores do not predict later job performance. What can be concluded?
options: The test is reliable but lacks predictive validity
The test is valid but lacks test-retest reliability
The test is both reliable and valid for selection
The test is neither reliable nor valid for selection
questions.explanation: Consistent scores show reliability. Validity for selection means scores predict job performance, which this test does not do, so it is of little use for choosing staff.

questions.stem: Why are references from previous employers often considered weak selection tools?
options: Referees are chosen by the applicant and tend to be positive
References always reveal the applicant's private medical information
References measure intelligence rather than job skills
References are scored by computer, so errors are common
questions.explanation: Applicants select referees likely to speak well of them, and referees may avoid criticism, so references often fail to distinguish between candidates.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of using a resume in personnel selection?
options: It gives a guaranteed accurate account of past performance
It measures personality traits with a standardised scale
It removes any need to interview shortlisted applicants
It quickly summarises qualifications for screening
questions.explanation: Resumes allow quick screening of qualifications and experience. However, they are written by applicants and may exaggerate, so they should be checked and combined with other assessments.

questions.stem: Which is an advantage of internet testing in personnel selection?
options: It guarantees the applicant completed the test without any help
It removes all privacy and data-security concerns for applicants
It ensures every applicant has the same internet speed and device
Many applicants in many places can be assessed cheaply
questions.explanation: Online testing is convenient and cost-effective for large pools. However, it is harder to confirm who completed the test, and technical differences may disadvantage some applicants.

questions.stem: Which is the main ethical issue with internet testing and online interviewing?
options: Applicants' personal data must be stored securely and used only as agreed
Online interviews always produce more valid results than face-to-face ones
Applicants cannot be asked for consent before an online test is given
Online tests must be kept secret from applicants until after selection
questions.explanation: Online assessment collects personal data that must be protected and used only for the purpose consented to. Unequal access to technology also raises fairness concerns.

questions.stem: Which is a disadvantage of online interviewing compared with face-to-face interviewing?
options: Technical problems and fewer non-verbal cues can affect judgements
Online interviews cannot be recorded or reviewed by other panel members
Online interviews always cost more than bringing applicants to the office
Online interviews can only be used for jobs in information technology
questions.explanation: Poor connections, delays and limited body language can disadvantage some applicants and affect how they are rated. Online interviews are usually cheaper and can be recorded.

questions.stem: An exit interview is used as a work-related measure mainly to:
options: select new applicants who will replace departing staff
rate the individual performance of employees who stay
measure the profit made by each department in a year
find out why employees are leaving the organisation
questions.explanation: Exit interviews ask departing employees about their reasons for leaving, which can reveal problems with conditions, management or culture that contribute to turnover.

questions.stem: Alderfer's ERG theory groups needs into which three categories?
options: esteem, recognition and personal goals
effort, reward and grades
energy, rest and generosity
existence, relatedness and growth
questions.explanation: Alderfer condensed Maslow's five levels into existence, relatedness and growth needs.

questions.stem: How does Alderfer's ERG theory differ from Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
options: It proposes that only pay and conditions motivate people at work
More than one level of need can motivate at once, and frustrated people may regress
Needs must be satisfied strictly in order from the bottom to the top of the hierarchy
It has more levels than Maslow, with self-actualisation divided into four parts
questions.explanation: ERG theory does not require needs to be met in a strict order and allows several to operate together. Its frustration-regression idea proposes that if a higher need is blocked, a person may focus more on a lower one.

questions.stem: According to Herzberg's two-factor theory, which is a hygiene factor?
options: achievement
salary
recognition
responsibility
questions.explanation: Hygiene factors, such as salary, working conditions, supervision and job security, prevent dissatisfaction when adequate but do not motivate on their own. Recognition, responsibility and achievement are motivators.

questions.stem: A company gives all staff a pay rise but motivation does not improve. Which explanation does Herzberg's theory offer?
options: Pay affects only existence needs, which are satisfied in all employees
Pay must be compared with a referent other before it can have any effect
Pay is a hygiene factor, so it reduces dissatisfaction but does not motivate
Pay is a motivator, so motivation should have risen if the rise was large enough
questions.explanation: Herzberg proposed that hygiene factors only prevent dissatisfaction. Motivation comes from motivators such as interesting work, responsibility and recognition. Comparing with others is Adams's equity theory.

questions.stem: An employee learns that a colleague doing the same work for the same hours is paid more, and starts putting in less effort. Which theory best explains this?
options: Herzberg's two-factor theory
Adams's equity theory
Locke's goal-setting theory
Holland's vocational theory
questions.explanation: Equity theory proposes that people compare their ratio of outcomes to inputs with a referent other. Perceived under-reward creates inequity, which people may reduce by lowering their inputs.

questions.stem: In Vroom's expectancy theory, instrumentality refers to the belief that:
options: the reward offered is personally valued
the reward is fair compared with others
good performance will lead to a reward
effort will lead to good performance
questions.explanation: Expectancy is the belief that effort leads to performance, instrumentality that performance leads to reward, and valence the value placed on the reward. Fairness compared with others is equity theory.

questions.stem: A salesperson believes extra effort will raise sales and that higher sales will earn a bonus, but he does not care about the bonus. According to Vroom, why is his motivation low?
options: The valence of the reward is low
The expectancy of success is low
The instrumentality is low
The hygiene factors are inadequate
questions.explanation: Motivation depends on expectancy, instrumentality and valence together. He believes effort works and that sales are rewarded, but a reward with low valence provides little motivation.

questions.stem: According to Locke's goal-setting theory, which goal is most likely to improve performance?
options: Try to have a good quarter if at all possible this time
Sell as much as you feel like selling this quarter
Raise sales by 10% this quarter, with weekly feedback
Do your very best with sales over the coming quarter
questions.explanation: Locke found that specific, challenging goals, accepted by the worker and supported by feedback, produce higher performance than vague goals such as do your best.

questions.stem: Which list gives the five core job characteristics in Hackman and Oldham's job design theory?
options: skill variety, task identity, task significance, autonomy, feedback
salary, security, supervision, conditions, company policy
existence, relatedness, growth, equity, expectancy
realistic, investigative, artistic, social, enterprising
questions.explanation: Hackman and Oldham proposed five core characteristics that create motivating work. Salary and conditions are Herzberg's hygiene factors, and the realistic to enterprising list is part of Holland's theory.

questions.stem: A worker on a production line only tightens one bolt on each car and never sees the finished vehicle. Which core job characteristic does never seeing the finished vehicle lower most directly?
options: task identity
feedback
autonomy
task significance
questions.explanation: Task identity is the extent to which a job involves completing a whole, identifiable piece of work. The job also lacks skill variety, but never seeing the finished product is about task identity.

questions.stem: In Hackman and Oldham's model, why would a job with no autonomy have very low motivating potential even if it is varied and significant?
options: Autonomy is a hygiene factor, so it prevents dissatisfaction only
Autonomy is added only once the job has been done for a year
Autonomy measures pay, which is the most important motivator
Autonomy multiplies the other factors, so a low score cuts the total
questions.explanation: In the motivating potential score, the average of skill variety, task identity and task significance is multiplied by autonomy and by feedback. A very low score on either multiplier keeps the total low.

questions.stem: Autonomy in a job leads to which critical psychological state in Hackman and Oldham's model?
options: experienced meaningfulness of the work
knowledge of the actual results of the work
a feeling of fairness compared with others
experienced responsibility for outcomes
questions.explanation: Autonomy produces experienced responsibility; skill variety, task identity and task significance produce experienced meaningfulness; feedback produces knowledge of results.
